verses.zh: 玛代族亚哈随鲁的儿子大利乌立为迦勒底国的王元年，
verses.en: In the first year of Darius[NOTE:1] son of Ahasuerus,[NOTE:2] who was of Median descent and who had been[NOTE:3] appointed king over the Babylonian[NOTE:4] empire—
notes: The identity of this Darius is a major problem in correlating the biblical material with the extra-biblical records of this period. Most modern scholars treat the reference as a mistaken allusion to Darius Hystaspes (ca. 522-486 b.c.). Others have maintained instead that this name is a reference to the Persian governor Gubaru. Still others understand the reference to be to the Persian king Cyrus (cf. 6:28, where the ו (vav) may be understood as vav explicativum, meaning “even”). Under either of these latter two interpretations, the first year of Darius would have been ca. 538 b.c. Daniel would have been approximately eighty-two years old at this time.
The LXX reads “Xerxes.” This is the reading used by some English versions (e.g., NIV, NCV, TEV, CEV). Most other English versions retain the Hebrew name “Ahasuerus.”

The present translation follows the MT in reading a Hophal (i.e., passive). Theodotion, the Syriac, and the Vulgate all presuppose the Hiphil (i.e., active). Even though this is the only occurrence of the Hophal of this verb in the Bible, there is no need to emend the vocalization to the Hiphil.
Heb “was made king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans.”
verses.commentary:
9:1-19 This is Daniel's prayer related to

- Jeremiah's prophecy of a seventy year exile from Jerusalem and the destroyed temple (vv. 1-2)

- Daniel's recognition of the reason for the exile which was the covenant violations of the people of Israel (v. 7)

- corporate confessional intercessory prayer to Israel's covenant God

- recognition that the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 had been triggered (v. 11)

- appeal is made to God's larger purpose for Israel (v. 19)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

9:1 "In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus of Median descent who was king over the kingdom
of the Chaldeans" See full note on this man at Dan. 5:31.

The real problem in Dan. 9:1 versus Dan. 5:31 is the addition of the father's name, Ahasuerus. This
name appears in the OT in Ezra 4:6 and Esther 1:1 as Esther's Persian husband, known by his Greek name,
Xerxes (LXX).

The name, like Darius, might be an honorific title (i.e., "mighty man" or "mighty eye,"
cf. BDB 31). As of this point in time scholarship knows nothing of this Chaldean ruler of Median descent. As
has happened so often already, archaeology has shed light on other perceived historical difficulties
(i.e. Belshazzar). So, let us keep searching!

▣ "of Median descent" If Darius, the son of Ahasuerus, is Cyrus, he was qualified to claim both
Median and Persian lineage.

▣ "who was made king" This is similar to Dan. 5:31. Was he made king by God or by human
authority? Obviously by both (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:7). Remember Dan. 2:20-23!

verses.zh: 就是他在位第一年，我但以理从书上得知耶和华的话临到先知耶利米，论耶路撒冷荒凉的年数，七十年为满。
verses.en: in the first year of his reign[NOTE:1] I, Daniel, came to understand from the sacred books[NOTE:2] that the number of years for the fulfilling of the desolation of Jerusalem,[NOTE:3] which had come as the Lord’s[NOTE:4] message to the prophet Jeremiah, would be 70 years.
notes: This phrase, repeated from v. 1, is absent in Theodotion.
Heb “books” or “scrolls.” The word “sacred” has been added to clarify that it refers to the Scriptures.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
The tetragrammaton (the four Hebrew letters that constitute the divine Name, YHWH) appears 8 times in this chapter and nowhere else in the book of Daniel.
verses.commentary:
9:2 "observed in the books the number of years which was revealed as the word of the Lord to
Jeremiah the prophet" This refers to Jer. 25:9-13 or 29:10, although another prophecy is made in
2 Chr. 36:21, where the years of captivity are prophesied as seventy in number because of the Jews'
failure to keep the sabbatical years mentioned in Lev. 26:33-35. This time sequence (70 years) is
important because it will be picked up on by the interpreting angel in Dan. 9:24 to describe a new period of
70 units which the people of God must endure.

It is possible that the 70 years refers to a complete life span. As God judged Israel with
a forty year wilderness wandering period for their unbelief (the age of those who could have been soldiers
at the time of the rebellion), He now judges His people with a judgment that covers the life span of an
entire generation of faithless Jews.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

▣ "for the completion of the desolations of Jerusalem" Jeremiah and Daniel use two different
Hebrew words for "desolation" (BDB 352 and BDB 1031). The one used here in Daniel (BDB 352) is also used in
connection with Jeremiah's prophecy about the exile of Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 25:9,11,18). These two terms
are both used in this chapter for the destroyed and profaned temple in Jerusalem (cf. Dan. 9:2 vs. 9:17,18).

verses.zh: 我便禁食，披麻蒙灰，定意向主　神祈祷恳求。
verses.en: So I turned my attention[NOTE:1] to the Lord God[NOTE:2] to implore him by prayer and requests, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “face.”
The Hebrew phrase translated “Lord God” here is אֲדֹנָי הָאֱלֹהִים (ʾadonay haʾelohim).
When lamenting, ancient Israelites would fast, wear sackcloth, and put ashes on their heads to show their sorrow and contrition.
verses.commentary:
9:3

NASB
"I gave my attention"

NKJV. JPSOA
"I set my face toward"

NRSV, REB
"I turned to"

TEV
"I prayed earnestly to"

NJB
"I turned my face to"

LXX
"I gave my face to"

Peshitta
"I lifted up my face to"

This is literally "I turned my face to the Lord." This idiom shows

- the personal intimacy of prayer. Prayer is not a monologue, but an intimate dialogue

- Daniel faced the ruined temple in Jerusalem when he prayed as if God's presence remained
there (cf. Dan. 6:10-11).

This is the first vision which was initiated by Daniel's questioning (cf. Joyce G. Baldwin,
Daniel, p. 162).

▣ "Lord" The NASB has "LORD," following some Hebrew
manuscripts. The MT of Dan. 9:3 has the Hebrew term Adon, which denotes "owner," "master," "husband"
and is usually translated "Lord." The covenant name YHWH (Lord; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR
DEITY, D.) does occur in Dan. 9:4. It occurs seven times in this chapter and nowhere else in Daniel. The
NASB (1995 Update) appropriately has "Lord" here in 9:3.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

▣ "God" This is the name Elohim. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

▣ "supplication" This Hebrew word (BDB 337) is used several times in chapter 9
(cf. Dan. 9:3,17,18,23). This term characterizes Daniel's prayer for the mercy of YHWH.

▣ "with fasting, sackcloth and ashes" These are all Jewish signs of mourning (e.g., Isa. 58:5;
Jonah 3:5-6; Esther 4:1-3).

- Fast ‒ Although not mentioned specifically in the writings of Moses, it was understood that
on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) that sorrow for sin would be symbolized by a day of fasting
by the whole nation. Throughout Jewish history national tragedies were commemorated by an
annual fast.

- Sackcloth ‒ This was a rough, plain cloth worn as a symbol of mourning.

- Ashes ‒ This seems to have started as a sign of mourning in Josh. 7:6 and developed into a
tradition (cf. 1 Sam. 4:12; 2 Sam. 1:2; 13:19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "I prayed to the Lord. . .O Lord" Notice the two different ways
"Lord" is spelled (i.e., one all capitals).

- The first, in all capitals translates the covenant name for Israel's God (YHWH), first mentioned in Gen. 2:4.
Elohim, God as Creator, Provider, and Sustainer of all life on this planet is used exclusively in Genesis 1.
God as Savior, Covenant Maker is introduced in Gen. 2:4 in the special creation of Adam.

- The second "Lord" is the Hebrew word for "owner," "master," "husband." The Jews pronounced this word as a
substitute for not pronouncing the holy name for God, YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. (Elohim)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D. (YHWH)

▣

NASB, TEV
"confessed"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, REB
"made confession"

LXX
"acknowledged Him"

This is the Hebrew word for "to throw" (BDB 392, KB 389; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 408, #13), used in the Hithpael
stem as an idiom for "confess" (cf. Lev. 16:21; 26:40; Num. 5:7; Ezra 10:1; Neh. 9:3; Dan. 9:3,20). Robert Young,
Analytical Concordance, p. 196, says it means "to throw out the hand" when the term refers to
"confessing YHWH's name" (LXX, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:33,35; 2 Chr. 6:24,26). Whether there was a physical gesture denoting
the confession of sin is uncertain, but probable.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NAME OF YHWH

▣ "Oh Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant and lovingkindness for those
who love Him and keep His commandments" This is a wonderful description of the covenant God.

- "The great" ‒ This is El ("God," BDB 42; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A.) with the ADJECTIVE "great" (BDB 152).

- "and awesome" ‒ This term's basic meaning is fear (BDB 431), but it is used here in the
Niphal for godly fear, respect or awe (e.g., Deut. 7:21; 10:17; Neh. 1:5; 4:14; 9:32; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR [OT]).

- "Who keeps covenant," The VERBAL (BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal PARTICIPLE)
is used twice and denotes that YHWH is faithful to His promises (cf. Num. 23:19; Mal. 3:6; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT).

- "Lovingkindness" ‒ This is the special covenant NOUN hesed (BDB 338),
used so often of YHWH's covenant loyalty (e.g., Deut. 7:9). See

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS

- "For those who love Him and keep His commandment" ‒ The VERBAL (BDB 12, KB 17,
Qal PARTICIPLE, which describes an ongoing action). This is the essence of the Mosaic
covenant (cf. Deut. 7:10; 27-29). Covenant love and loyalty on God's part is meant to reproduce
itself in His covenant people (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP). The NT accentuates God's faithfulness (cf. 2 Tim. 3:13) amidst
human faithlessness.

verses.zh: 我向耶和华―我的　神祈祷、认罪，说：「主啊，大而可畏的　神，向爱主、守主诫命的人守约施慈爱。
verses.en: I prayed to the Lord my God, confessing in this way: “O Lord,[NOTE:1] great and awesome God who is faithful to his covenant[NOTE:2] with those who love him and keep his commandments,
notes: The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here and in vv. 7, 9, 15, 16, and 19 is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).
Heb “who keeps the covenant and the loyal love.” The expression is a hendiadys.

verses.zh: 我们犯罪作孽，行恶叛逆，偏离你的诫命典章，
verses.en: we have sinned! We have done what is wrong and wicked; we have rebelled by turning away from your commandments and standards.
verses.commentary:
9:5 "we have sinned" Notice the recurrent theme, Dan. 9:5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17. Daniel
identifies himself with his people and makes confession, as did Moses (e.g., Exod. 32:32; Num. 11:2; 21:7)
and Isaiah (e.g., Isa. 6:5).

What a list of willful covenant disobedience! Israel had violated the covenant over and
over again. The Assyrian and Babylonian exiles and the complete destruction of Jerusalem and the temple
were the consequences.

- "Sinned" (BDB 306, KB 305, Qal PERFECT) ‒ the basic meaning is missing the mark.

- "Committed iniquity" (BDB 731, KB 796 Qal PERFECT) ‒ the basic meaning is guilty acts ("to be bent"
or "to make crooked").

- "Acted wickedly" (BDB 957, KB 1294, Hiphil PERFECT) ‒ the basic meaning is to be loose or disjointed
(cf. Dan. 9:5).

- "Rebelled" (BDB 597, KB 632, Qal PERFECT) ‒ the basic meaning is bold in acts of known disobedience
(cf. Dan. 9:9).

- "turning aside" (BDB 693, KB 747, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) ‒ the basic meaning is to knowingly depart from a clear
path (cf. Dan. 9:11).

verses.zh: 没有听从你仆人众先知奉你名向我们君王、首领、列祖，和国中一切百姓所说的话。
verses.en: We have not paid attention to your servants the prophets, who spoke by your authority[NOTE:1] to our kings, our leaders, and our ancestors,[NOTE:2] and to all the inhabitants[NOTE:3] of the land as well.
notes: Heb “in your name.” Another option is to translate: “as your representatives.”
Heb “our fathers” (also in vv. 8, 16). The Hebrew term translated “father” can refer to more distant relationships such as grandfathers or ancestors.
Heb “people.”
verses.commentary:
9:6 "we have not listened to Your servants the prophets" The Jews (kings, princes, ancestors, and
all the common people) were not ignorant or uninformed about God's covenant will. They had the writings
of Moses, the miracles of the Exodus, the victories of the conquest and the fulfillment of the Abrahamic
promise of land, but they would not be faithful (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:13-15; Jer. 44:4,5,21; Hosea 11:2).

Israel's disobedience highlights God's faithfulness and mercy. I have added my exegetical notes
from Exodus 32:9.

Exod. 32:9 "an obstinate people" This is literally "stiff necked" (BDB 766 I CONSTRUCT
BDB 904 and 791, cf. Exod. 33:3,5; 34:9; Deut. 9:6,13; 31:27; Ezek. 2:4; Acts 7:51) and is used of domestic
animals that will not respond to a bridle or yoke.

This description (by YHWH) of Israel is very important. YHWH did not choose them because of their
morality, number, or character (cf. Deut. 9:6; 10:16; 31:27; Ezek. 2:4). As a matter of fact, His character
is fully revealed in light of their character. If He was patient with them; He will be patient with us!

verses.zh: 主啊，你是公义的，我们是脸上蒙羞的；因我们犹大人和耶路撒冷的居民，并以色列众人，或在近处，或在远处，被你赶到各国的人，都得罪了你，正如今日一样。
verses.en: “You are righteous,[NOTE:1] O Lord, but we are humiliated this day[NOTE:2]—the people[NOTE:3] of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and all Israel, both near and far away in all the countries in which you have scattered them because they have behaved unfaithfully toward you.
notes: Heb “to you (belongs) righteousness.”
Heb “and to us (belongs) shame of face like this day.”
Heb “men.”
verses.commentary:
9:7 "righteousness belongs to You" The term "righteousness" (cf. Dan. 9:14,16) is the Hebrew word
(BDB 841-842) for a "measuring reed," "ruler," or "standard." God Himself is the standard of judgment. He chose this
imagery to establish His character as Judge.

Fallen humanity's only hope of meeting God's standard is the imputed righteousness of Jesus
Christ (cf. Lev. 19:2; Matt. 5:48; 2 Cor. 5:21). That is why the OT is simply a school-master to lead us
until Christ (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-38; Gal. 3:19-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

▣

NASB, NRSV
"open shame"

NKJV, LXX
"shame of face"

TEV
"disgrace on ourselves"

NJB
"the look of shame"

JPSOA
"shame is on us"

Peshitta
"shame is ours"

As covenant loyalty (Dan. 9:4) and righteousness belong to the faithful God, so covenant
disloyalty and open shame belong to His faithless people.

This Hebrew construct (BDB 102 plus DBD 815) is translated "confusion of face" or "shame of
face" (cf. Dan. 9:8). The same construction is found in 2 Chr. 32:21. This phrase refers to the exiles
of Israel being taken from the Promised Land. This damaged God's reputation among the nations. He wanted
to bless Israel and use her as a light to bring the world to Himself (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6), but
their continual covenant infidelity resulted in judgment for them and a misunderstanding of YHWH by the
world (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣

NASB
"as it is this day"

NKJV
"as it is this day"

NRSV, MT
"as at this day"

TEV
——

NJB
"we wear today"

REB
"now as ever"

JPSOA
;"to this very day"

LXX
"on this day"

Peshitta
"as to this day"

The best parallel to help understand the theology of this phrase is Ezek. 36:22-36, which
is really a description of "the grace-based New Covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34. The Mosaic performance-based covenant
(i.e., "if. . .then") could not be kept by fallen humans, even humans with divine revelation (cf. Romans 9).

▣ "to the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and all Israel" This is referring to
"the desolations" in Dan. 9:2. God allowed Assyria (cf. Isa. 10:5) and Babylon (cf. Jer. 51:20) to exile
His own people. God uses foreign nations to bring judgment on His faithless people (as He does in A.D.
66-70).

▣ "those who are near by and those who are far away in all the countries to which You have
driven them" God's covenant people, the descendants of Abraham to whom God promised a land
(cf. Gen. 12:1-3, etc.), were taken out of the promised land and scattered among the nations because
of their idolatry and violations of the covenant (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:46; Lev. 26; Deut. 28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

verses.zh: 主啊，我们和我们的君王、首领、列祖因得罪了你，就都脸上蒙羞。
verses.en: O Lord, we have been humiliated[NOTE:1]—our kings, our leaders, and our ancestors—because we have sinned against you.
notes: Heb “to us (belongs) shame of face.”

verses.zh: 主―我们的　神是怜悯饶恕人的，我们却违背了他，
verses.en: Yet the Lord our God is compassionate and forgiving,[NOTE:1] even though we have rebelled against him.
notes: Heb “to the Lord our God (belong) compassion and forgiveness.”
verses.commentary:
9:9 "To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness" The term "compassion" (BDB 933) may be
imagery from the word "womb," thereby speaking of family love. God often describes His ways with humanity
by means of familial images (father, kinsman redeemer, parents, family, children).

There are only a few places in the OT where the character of God is delineated with such
clarity (cf. Exod. 34:6-7; Ps. 103:8-14; Joel 2:13; Neh. 9:17-21). Sinful mankind's only hope is the
unchanging (cf. Mal. 3:6), merciful character of God (cf. Dan. 9:18; Mal. 3:6)!

The term "forgiveness" used here is a rare form (PLURAL ABSTRACT, INTENSIVE,
"abundantly forgive") of the word (BDB 699); it is also used in Neh. 9:17. The unemphasized form is found
in Dan. 9:19.

verses.zh: 也没有听从耶和华―我们　神的话，没有遵行他藉仆人众先知向我们所陈明的律法。
verses.en: We have not obeyed[NOTE:1] the Lord our God by living according to[NOTE:2] his laws[NOTE:3] that he set before us through his servants the prophets.
notes: Heb “paid attention to the voice of,” which is an idiomatic expression for obedience (cf. NASB “nor have we obeyed the voice of”).
Heb “to walk in.”
The LXX and Vulgate have the singular.
verses.commentary:
9:10 "through His servants the prophets" When we see the English word "prophets," we think of
Isaiah ‒ Malachi, but Judaism believed that prophets wrote Scripture, so

- Moses is a prophet (cf. Deuteronomy 18)

- the history books of the OT (Joshua ‒ Kings) are written by prophets and are called "the Former
Prophets" by the rabbis

This phrase includes all the Old Testament up to Daniel's day (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:13-15; 18:12).

verses.zh: 以色列众人都犯了你的律法，偏行，不听从你的话；因此，在你仆人摩西律法上所写的咒诅和誓言都倾在我们身上，因我们得罪了　神。
verses.en: “All Israel has broken[NOTE:1] your law and turned away by not obeying you.[NOTE:2] Therefore you have poured out on us the judgment solemnly threatened[NOTE:3] in the law of Moses the servant of God, for we have sinned against you.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “transgressed.” The Hebrew verb has the primary sense of crossing a boundary, in this case, God’s law.
Heb “by not paying attention to your voice.”

Heb “the curse and the oath that is written.” The term “curse” refers here to the judgments threatened in the Mosaic law (see Deut 28) for rebellion. The expression “the curse and the oath” is probably a hendiadys (cf. Num 5:21; Neh 10:29) referring to the fact that the covenant with its threatened judgments was ratified by solemn oath and made legally binding upon the covenant community.
Heb “him.”
verses.commentary:
9:11 "transgressed" The word appears here and in Dan. 8:23. Its basic meaning is to go beyond a
known boundary (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PERFECT).

Notice the series of expressions used in Dan. 9:11 to show Israel's covenant breaking.

- transgressed ("pass over," BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PERFECT

- turned aside (BDB 693, KB 747, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE

- not obeying (cf. Dan. 9:14; "not listen," BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- we have sinned (cf. Dan. 9:5,15; BDB 306, KB 305, Qal PERFECT)

Also notice in Dan. 9:11 what they sinned against.

- "Your law"

- "Your voice"

- "against Him" (cf. Dan. 9:8,9)

All sin is ultimately against a personal God. We have not just broken rules, we have broken
our relationship with the One in whose image we were fashioned (cf. Gen. 1:26-27)! Sin destroys the essence
of our created purpose-fellowship with God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN IN THE OT

▣ "the curse" The term "curse" (BDB 46) can also be translated "oath" (cf. Neh. 10:29). This
covenantal terminology goes back to the covenant "curses and blessings" of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29, where Israel
promises to obey God's word (cf. Deut. 29:11-13). However, if they rebel and disobey, God's oath becomes a
curse (cf. Deut. 29:18,19,20; 30:7; 2 Chr. 34:24; Jer. 29:18-19).

▣ "Moses the servant of God" See

verses.zh: 他使大灾祸临到我们，成就了警戒我们和审判我们官长的话；原来在普天之下未曾行过像在耶路撒冷所行的。
verses.en: He has carried out his threats[NOTE:1] against us and our rulers[NOTE:2] who were over[NOTE:3] us by bringing great calamity on us—what has happened to Jerusalem has never been equaled under all heaven!
notes: Heb “he has fulfilled his word(s), which he spoke.”
Heb “our judges.”
Heb “who judged.”
verses.commentary:
9:12 "He has confirmed His word which He has spoken" God's promises and His judgments all come true
(cf. Isa. 40:8; 45:23; 46:10-11; 55:11). The trustworthiness of God's character rests on the trustworthiness
of His word!

Yet, in making this statement there are some mitigating circumstances.

- the "if. . .then" nature of conditional covenants fully expects repentance to make a difference (i.e., Jonah and Nineveh)

verses.zh: 这一切灾祸临到我们身上是照摩西律法上所写的，我们却没有求耶和华―我们　神的恩典，使我们回头离开罪孽，明白你的真理。
verses.en: Just as it is written in the law of Moses, so all this calamity has come on us. Still we have not tried to pacify[NOTE:1] the Lord our God by turning back from our sin and by seeking wisdom[NOTE:2] from your reliable moral standards.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “we have not pacified the face of.”
Or “by gaining insight.”
Heb “by your truth.” The Hebrew term does not refer here to abstract truth, however, but to the reliable moral guidance found in the covenant law (see vv 10-11).
verses.commentary:
9:13 "turning from" This is the main VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) for the
theological concept of turning back to God in repentance.

verses.zh: 所以耶和华留意使这灾祸临到我们身上，因为耶和华―我们的　神在他所行的事上都是公义；我们并没有听从他的话。
verses.en: The Lord was mindful of the calamity, and he brought it on us. For the Lord our God is just[NOTE:1] in all he has done,[NOTE:2] and we have not obeyed him.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “righteous.”
Heb “in all his deeds that he has done.”
Heb “we have not listened to his voice.”
verses.commentary:
9:14

NASB
"the Lord has kept the calamity in store and brought it on us"

NKJV
"the Lord has kept the disaster in mind"

NRSV, LXX
"the Lord kept watch over this calamity until he brought it upon us"

God deals with His people as a loving parent.

verses.zh: 主―我们的　神啊，你曾用大能的手领你的子民出埃及地，使自己得了名，正如今日一样。我们犯了罪，作了恶。

verses.commentary:
9:15 "who brought Your people out of the land of Egypt" The Exodus fulfilled God's promise of
Gen. 15:12-21. The symbolism from Genesis 15 conveys the concept that God and God alone can accomplish
this act of deliverance and promise (i.e., unconditional covenant). In point of fact the OT is as much an account of YHWH's grace and
mercy as is the NT. The character of God has not changed (cf. Mal.3:6), but the covenant requirements have
been modified because of mankind's (even redeemed mankind's) inability to keep the covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34;
Ezek. 36:22-36). The covenant is still conditional, but structured so that the Messiah's performance
replaces human performance as the means and basis of redemption (cf. Isaiah 53; Eph. 2:8-9; 2 Cor. 5:21).

▣ "with a mighty hand" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND, #2, d.

▣ "and have made a name for Yourself" God wanted to use the family of Abraham to reach all the
world in reconciliation (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6). The Exodus was for the ultimate purpose of world evangelism (cf. Exod. 9:16;
Neh. 9:10) as much as a national promise!

notes: Or “righteousness.”

verses.commentary:
9:16 "in accordance with all Your righteous acts" Notice how Daniel uses YHWH's character,

- in Dan. 9:7 Daniel attributes righteousness to God

- in 9:14 Daniel elicits the covenant claim, "the Lord our God is righteous"

- now in 9:16 Daniel appeals to the character of God (cf. Dan. 9:17,19)

not the disobedience of His people (cf. Dan. 9:18), as the reason to restore Israel (cf. Dan. 9:20; Jer. 32:30-35),
so as to complete their calling of being a light to the nations!

notes: Heb “hear.” Here the verb refers to hearing favorably, accepting the prayer and responding positively.

Heb “for the sake of my Lord.” Theodotion has “for your sake.” Cf. v. 19.

9:17 "for Your sake, O Lord" This is repeated in Dan. 9:19. Daniel supplicates YHWH to act so as to

verses.zh: 我的　神啊，求你侧耳而听，睁眼而看，眷顾我们荒凉之地和称为你名下的城。我们在你面前恳求，原不是因自己的义，乃因你的大怜悯。
verses.en: Listen attentively,[NOTE:1] my God, and hear! Open your eyes and look on our desolated ruins[NOTE:2] and the city called by your name.[NOTE:3] For it is not because of our own righteous deeds that we are praying to you,[NOTE:4] but because your compassion is abundant.
notes: Many translations have “called by your name,” but that is a Hebrew idiom meaning “belongs to you.” Cf. v. 19. This expression implies that God is the owner of his city, Jerusalem. Note the use of the idiom in 2 Sam 12:28; Isa 4:1; Amos 9:12.
See the note on this expression in v. 18.
Heb “the holy mountain of my God.”
Heb “speaking in prayer.”
verses.commentary:
9:18 "ear. . .eyes" This is anthropomorphic imagery to describe Israel's Deity as a person. YHWH is the eternal
Spirit present throughout His creation. However, He is also a person. Humans only have vocabulary based on their
experience of this planet. So, they use personal terms to address and converse with God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "not. . .on account of any merits of our own, but on account of Your great compassion" Daniel is
praying much like Moses, in that he appeals to God's character (cf. Dan. 9:17,19) for forgiveness and
unmerited deliverance to Jerusalem, the temple, and the people as a whole (cf. Dan. 9:19), not based on any deserved
or attained righteousness on Israel's part. This is the OT incipient concept of justification by grace
through faith (cf. Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3; Gal. 3:6; Eph. 2:8-9).

verses.zh: 我说话，祷告，承认我的罪和本国之民以色列的罪，为我　神的圣山，在耶和华―我　神面前恳求。
verses.en: While I was still speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel and presenting my request before the Lord my God concerning his holy mountain[NOTE:1]—
notes: The Hebrew expression מֻעָף בִּיעָף (muʿaf biʿaf) is very difficult. The issue is whether the verb derives from עוּף (ʿuf, “to fly”) or from יָעַף (yaʿaf, “to be weary”). Many ancient versions and modern commentators take the first of these possibilities and understand the reference to be to the swift flight of the angel Gabriel in his coming to Daniel. The words more likely refer to the extreme weariness, not of the angel, but of Daniel (cf. 7:28; 8:27; 10:8-9, 16-17; also NASB).
verses.commentary:
9:20 Notice all the PARTICIPLES, which basically refer to the same act.

- speaking (Piel)

- praying (Hithpael)

- confessing (Hithpael)

- presenting (Hiphil)

- speaking (Piel, v. 21)

▣ "the holy mountain of my God" This refers to Mt. Moriah in Jerusalem (Jerusalem was built
on sevenhills), on which Solomon's temple was built (cf. 2 Chr. 3:1). This was the same mountain on which
Abraham offered Isaac (cf. Gen. 22:2) and this same mountain was later a place where David offered a
sacrifice to stop the judgment of God (cf. 2 Sam. 24:18-25; 1 Chr. 21:18-27).

verses.zh: 我正祷告的时候，先前在异象中所见的那位加百列，奉命迅速飞来，约在献晚祭的时候，按手在我身上。
verses.en: yes, while I was still praying,[NOTE:1] the man Gabriel, whom I had seen previously[NOTE:2] in a vision, was approaching me in my state of extreme weariness,[NOTE:3] around the time of the evening offering.
notes: Heb “he instructed and spoke with me.” The expression is a verbal hendiadys.
Or “a precious treasure”; KJV “greatly beloved”; NASB, NIV “highly esteemed.”
This sentence is perhaps a compound hendiadys (“give serious consideration to the revelatory vision”).
verses.commentary:
9:21 "then the man Gabriel" This is a messenger angel. His name means "man of God" (BDB 150, cf. Dan. 8:16).
He is only one of two angels whose names are mentioned in the Bible, Gabriel and Michael.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "in my extreme weariness" Some commentators link this to

- the angel Gabriel, who was wearied by his swift flight (Aramaism, BDB 419, KB 421, see NIDOTTE, vol. 3,
pp. 390, 395; NET Bible, p. 1551, #8)

- some see it as referring to Daniel's weariness (cf. Dan. 7:28; 8:27; 10:8-9,16-17)

- Since I do not think angels get tired (possibly Dan. 10:12-13), it probably refers to Daniel.

▣ "about the time of the evening offering" Remember, the temple was destroyed. There were no
offerings. The evening offering would have been about 3:00 p.m. Daniel kept the temple ritual alive by
continuing his habit of prayer (cf. Dan. 6:10)!

verses.zh: 他指教我说：「但以理啊，现在我出来要使你有智慧，有聪明。
verses.en: He spoke with me, instructing me as follows:[NOTE:1] “Daniel, I have now come to impart understanding to you.
notes: Heb “sevens.” Elsewhere the term is used of a literal week (a period of seven days); cf. Gen 29:27-28; Exod 34:22; Lev 12:5; Num 28:26; Deut 16:9-10; 2 Chr 8:13; Jer 5:24; Dan 10:2-3. Gabriel unfolds the future as if it were a calendar of successive weeks. Most understand the reference here as seventy “sevens” of years, or a total of 490 years.
verses.commentary:
9:22 "to give you insight with understanding" The Hebrew word "insight" (BDB 968) is used in several
senses.

- positively of wisdom of Daniel in Dan. 1:4,17; 9:25

- negatively of the craftiness of the little horn in Dan. 8:25

- negatively of unfaithful Israel in Dan. 9:13

- positively of restored Israel in Dan. 11:33,35

- positively of believers of the end-time period in Dan. 12:3,10

The Hebrew term "understanding" (BDB 108) is used in Dan. 1:20; 8:15; 9:22; 10:1. Daniel
was gifted by God and enabled by angelic interpreters to grasp the meaning of the symbolic visions. This
particular explanation relates to the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy from Dan. 9:2.

The question I continue to ask in connection with the genre of both Daniel, Zechariah,
and Revelation is, "Did these authors receive a message from God and then structure it as apocalyptic
literature or did they receive it as structured symbols?" Could both be true? Does God suddenly change
the form of revelation from prophetic models to apocalyptic models? I suppose I believe that these inspired
human authors structured their messages in symbolic, dramatic, imaginative, figurative ways. The message
is from God, but its presentation comes through inspired humans using different literary genres.

verses.zh: 你初恳求的时候，就发出命令，我来告诉你，因你大蒙眷爱；所以你要思想明白这以下的事和异象。
verses.en: At the beginning of your requests a message went out, and I have come to convey it to you, for you are of great value in God’s sight.[NOTE:1] Therefore consider the message and understand the vision:[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “to finish.” The present translation reads the Qere (from the root תָּמַם, tamam) with many witnesses. The Kethib has “to seal up” (from the root הָתַם, hatam), a confusion with a reference later in the verse to sealing up the vision.
The present translation reads the Qere (singular), rather than the Kethib (plural).
verses.commentary:
9:23 "the command was issued" This is literally, "a word went out" (BDB 422, KB 425, Qal
PERFECT). It may have come from

- the powerful angel as in Dan. 8:16

- God (cf. Isa. 45:23; 55:11)

Even before Daniel finished praying heaven had responded!

verses.zh: 「为你本国之民和你圣城，已经定了七十个七。要止住罪过，除净罪恶，赎尽罪孽，引进（或译：彰显）永义，封住异象和预言，并膏至圣者（者：或译所）。

notes: The Hebrew phrase לְכַלֵּא (lekhalleʾ) is apparently an alternative (metaplastic) spelling of the root כָּלָה (kalah, “to complete, finish”), rather than a form of כָּלָא (kalaʾ, “to shut up, restrain”), as has sometimes been supposed.
Or “everlasting.”
The act of sealing in the OT is a sign of authentication (cf. 1 Kgs 21:8 and Jer 32:10, 11, 44).
Heb “vision and prophecy.” The expression is a hendiadys.
Or “the most holy place” (NASB, NLT); or “a most holy one”; or “the most holy one,” though the expression is used of places or objects elsewhere, not people.
Or “decree” (NASB, NIV84); or “word” (NAB, NRSV, NIV11).
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
The word “arrives” is added in the translation for clarification.
verses.commentary:
9:24-27 This passage has a parallel or poetic aspect (series of INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS)
and is translated into poetic lines by NJB (Dan. 9:24-27) and NAB (9:22-26) translations, but not by most
English versions.

This is one of the most specific, yet debated, passages in the OT.

- How many people are spoken about and who are they?

- Have we switched genres from apocalyptic, fuzzy, symbolic, imaginative literature (Daniel 7; 8) to a very specific, historical
prophecy (Dan. 9:24-27 and chapter 11)?

- Are the details meant to be seen as foreshadowing

- interbiblical period (Antiochus IV)

- Jesus' day (Jewish War, A.D. 66-70)

- end-time events and people (Second Coming)

Does this vision have any connection

- to the vision of Daniel 8 and Dan. 11:1-35

- to an extension going back to and extending the little horn of the fourth kingdom (anti-God person/empire; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANTICHRIST) of Daniel 7
and Dan. 11:36-45? What is the literary context; to which historical setting?

- A third option is to see it as referring to the time of Jesus (His Incarnation and earthly life), which would limit it to the fifth kingdom,
the Messianic Kingdom, of Dan. 2:35, 44-45; 7:9-10, 13-14,18,22,27. This is the option I feel most comfortable with at this point in
my study (i.e., Partial Preterism). Passages like this must remain tentative!

This paragraph functions theologically in several ways.

- God has punished His own people. Sin is an ongoing problem.

- God will forgive and restore His people. Forgiveness and restoration are always possible.

- More problems remain for His people in the future.

- Messiah is coming, but He will be a suffering servant (cf. Isaiah 53), a wounded shepherd
(cf. Zechariah 12-13)

- God will judge those who attack His Messiah and His people.

One of my concerns with this context is that it is presented in the OT prophetic terms of
the "land" promises to Abraham (Genesis 12;15;16), but the NT expands this into a universal perspective!
See SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY ARE OT
COVENANT PROMISES SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?. Daniel is familiar with the Gentile kings to
whom YHWH has revealed Himself and they have praised Him. God's people are wider than racial Jews
(cf. Rom. 2:28-29; 9:6; Gal. 3:7-9,29; 6:16; 1 Pet. 2:5,9; 3:6; Rev. 1:6).

At this point please turn to Contextual Insights for Daniel 11 and read F, which deals with
the nature of apocalyptic literature taken from Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language
of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic by D. Brent Sandy, pp. 156-158.

9:24 "Seventy weeks" The Hebrew phrase (BDB 988; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 20-23,34-36) is literally "seventy units of seven" (weeks or Sabbaths).
Numerals were usually FEMININE PLURAL, but here they are MASCULINE PLURAL and
this is unusual, possibly to denote its symbolic nature. This "seventy units of seven" relates to the seventy
years of Jeremiah's prophecy noted in Dan. 9:2 (but may not be the same use of the number seventy). Daniel is being told
that there would be a another period in Israel's history when the temple would be destroyed again (similar to Ezekiel 38-39),
but he was to remember that God was in control of all human history and that He would bring creation to its divine purpose (i.e, Dan. 2:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

▣ "have been decreed" This Hebrew term "decree" (BDB 367, KB 364, Niphal PERFECT)
is found only here in the OT (there are three Aramaic terms translated "decree" in Dan. 2:4-7:28, but none relate to this Hebrew form).
It is related to an Aramaic term which meant "to cut," "cut off," or "decide."

The "decree" of Dan. 9:24 is parallel to the "decree" (literally "word," BDB 182) of
Dan. 9:25! This whole section of Daniel deals with

- the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 B.C. because
of Israel/Judah's sins and continued violations of the Mosaic Covenant

- Jeremiah's prediction (cf. Jer. 25:12; 29:10) of a 70 year exile of God's covenant people from the Land of Canaan

- the revelation to Daniel by an angel that Jerusalem would be restored by a decree (v. 25)

- however, another prediction is given about a future second destruction of the restored city and temple related to 70 weeks (possibly years, 490 years)

- verses 26-27 deal primarily with the future destruction of the restored city and temple by Titus in A.D. 70. (I have
come to believe that the Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation refer to this temporal "coming": see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.). This destruction ends the sacrificial system of the Mosaic Covenant. A
new covenant begins!

- There is no textual hint of an end-time antichrist or future building of the temple. For a good discussion of Preterism, see Kenneth
Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell.

These insights have come to me from Steve Gregg (www.thenarrowpath.com and his YouTube videos on
"Dispensationalism," "The Modern State of Israel," and "The Olivet Discourse" ). I was not aware of how much
my eschatological understanding had been affected by my historical setting and not exegesis. Texts have priority, not theological systems
(i.e., dispensational premillennial). I have become convinced that the vast majority of OT prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus' first coming
(see Fee and Stuart, How To Read The Bible For All Its Worth, p. 182):

Less than 2 percent of OT prophecy is Messianic. Less than 5 percent describes the new covenant age. Less than 1
percent concerns events yet to come in our time."

The NT is about Jesus and not about Israel!

Connected to this restoration is God's eternal redemptive plan (cf. Dan. 9:24), which involved the Messiah's being "cut off"
(cf. Dan. 9:26; Zech. 9-14) and Jerusalem destroyed again (cf. Dan. 9:26; Ezekiel 38-39; Olivet Discourse, and Revelation).

If one takes the historical period from the permission of Artaxerxes for Nehemiah to return
to Jerusalem and rebuild the walls of the city in 445 B.C. and if one assumes that "seventy
weeks" refers to 490 years; and if one calculates the end of the 69th week as 483 years, then
one comes very close to the date of the beginning of Jesus'

- ministry (i.e., baptism)

- triumphal entry into Jerusalem

- crucifixion (the cutting off of the Messiah)

There have been three major theories about this decree related to Persian monarchs:

- Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, allowed all captive people to return to their homes in
538 B.C. (cf. Isa. 44:26-28; Ezra 1). This assumes Darius of Daniel 6 is Cyrus.

- Artaxerxes to Ezra in 458 B.C. allowed more priests and Levites to return to
Jerusalem with Ezra (cf. in Aramaic, Ezra 7:11-26)

- Artaxerxes to Nehemiah, 445 B.C. allowed Nehemiah to go to Jerusalem for the explicit purpose
of rebuilding the walls (cf. Neh. 1:3; 2:3-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "for your people and your holy city" This decree refers to Jerusalem, but which time-frame?

- Ezra-Nehemiah in the Persian period

- Maccabees in the Greek period

- Jesus in the Roman period

- end-time

- or is this a recurrent pattern through human history

- covenant disobedience on the part of God's people

- the anger of unbelieving humanity against God and His people

It seems to me that #3 is the textual choice. See Four Views On the Book of Revelation, pp. 35-92.

It is interesting that John Darby (i.e., Dispensationalism) sees the following six things as not being fulfilled
in Jesus' ministry, therefore, they must be done in a future time. In order to do this, they insert several long, unexpected gaps in history.

- in Daniel 2, between the fourth metal (i.e., Rome) legs and feet

- in Daniel 7, fourth beast, little horn

- in Daniel 9, between 69th week and 70th week

- in Isa. 6:1 and 61:2

These textual assumptions (i.e., gaps) are only made because of a theological system. There is no hint of a
2,000 plus year gap in any of these contexts. No original reader would have suspected these gaps!

The first part of this Hebrew construct means "to finish," "to complete" (BDB 477-8,
KB 476, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, from an Aramaic root "to cease" or "to perish,"
cf. 2 Chr. 31:3; Ezra 9:1).

H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, pp. 411-412, says this is the only occurrence
of a different Hebrew VERB (BDB 480, KB 476) in the Piel form and should be translated
"to restrain completely." Both the NASB and NIV note this possibility in a footnote, but use the first option
in the translation.

The term "transgression" (BDB 833, "rebel," "revolt," "transgress") is used in Daniel 8 and 9
of several different people and sins.

- sins of the Jewish people (cf. Dan. 8:12-13,23, a different word in Dan. 9:11)

- sins of Jewish leadership that helped Antiochus IV (cf. Dan. 8:12-13,23)

- sins of Antiochus IV (cf. Dan. 8:12-13,23)

Daniel 9:24 is not referring to one particular time or kind of sinning or rebellion, but
to the problem of sin, particularly by His own covenant people, Israel. Jesus' condemnation of Judaism, found in

verses.en: So know and understand:From the issuing of the command[NOTE:1] to restore and rebuild Jerusalem[NOTE:2] until an anointed one, a prince arrives,[NOTE:3] there will be a period of seven weeks[NOTE:4] and sixty-two weeks.It will again be built,[NOTE:5] with plaza and moat,but in distressful times.
notes: The accents in the MT indicate disjunction at this point, which would make it difficult, if not impossible, to identify the “anointed one/prince” of this verse as messianic. The reference in v. 26 to the sixty-two weeks as a unit favors the MT accentuation, not the traditional translation. If one follows the MT accentuation, one may translate “From the going forth of the message to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed one, a prince arrives, there will be a period of seven weeks. During a period of sixty-two weeks it will again be built, with plaza and moat, but in distressful times.” The present translation follows a traditional reading of the passage that deviates from the MT accentuation. tn Heb “sevens” (also later in this line and in v. 26).
Heb “it will return and be built.” The expression is a verbal hendiadys.

The expression have nothing is difficult. Presumably it refers to an absence of support or assistance for the anointed one at the time of his “cutting off.” The KJV rendering “but not for himself,” apparently suggesting a vicarious death, cannot be defended.

Some witnesses (e.g., the Syriac) understand a passive verb and the preposition עִם (ʿim, “with) rather than the noun עַם (ʿam, “people”), thus reading “the city and the sanctuary will be destroyed with the coming prince.”
The words “will come speedily” are not in the Hebrew text but have been added in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
9:25 "from the issuing of a decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem" If this is to be understood
historically then it relates to

- Cyrus' decree for all the exiled nations under the domination of Assyria and Babylon to return
home and restore their national temples (i.e., so they can all pray for Cyrus; 538 B.C.), cf Ezra 1:3; 6:3

- Artaxerxes' decrees to Ezra (458 B.C.) and especially to Nehemiah
(445 B.C.) related to the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem cf. Ezra 7:11-26.

It is just possible that the decree refers to God's sovereign redemptive plan (i.e., prophetic "word," BDB 182;
NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 913, #2) referred to as a decree (cf. Jer. 25:9-13). E. J. Young, The Prophecy of Daniel: A Commentary,
p. 201, asserts that it is God who issues the word/decree which shows the parallel with Dan. 9:23 (both use the same Hebrew
term, "word," [BDB 182], cf. Jer. 25:13). God's plans are worked out on earth through the decrees of pagan
kings (cf. Dan. 2:21; Luke 2:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "Messiah, the Prince" This is literally "an anointed, a prince." There is no ARTICLE. and no
capitalization from the Hebrew text. Many scholars and commentators
have understood "anointed one" to refer to Cyrus II (cf. Isa. 41:2,25; 44:28-45:7; 46:11; 48:15) whom
YHWH used to restore His people to the Promised Land. These interpreters then relate Dan. 9:26-27 to
the time and activities of Antiochus IV.

The reason that some scholars deny that this phrase refers to the Messiah (cf. NET Bible,
Second Beta Ed., p. 1551, footnote 23) is because there is an accent mark (athnach) in the Hebrew
Masoretic Text, which denotes a disjunction. However,

- in the first place, the accent marks of the MT are not inspired, but are Jewish rabbinical traditions

- second, this mark does not always denote a complete stop, but here possibly accents the distinction between
the time period of seven weeks and sixty-two weeks (cf. Christology of the Old Testament, by E. W. Hengstenberg,
pp.415-417; H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, pp. 417-426; and Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 318-320).

For me this refers to Jesus "the" Messiah (cf. Dan. 7:13). In verse 26 this title is split
into two different persons. The first phrase, "the anointed one" refers to Jesus, while the second phrase,
"the people of the Prince," apparently refers" to Titus, the Roman general who destroyed Jerusalem in
A.D. 70.

If this apocalyptic language has a multiple fulfillment aspect then surely an end-time
context is possible. The nature of evil and rebellion in both humans and angels remains constant, but
the historical details do not. This is not a specific prophecy, but an apocalyptic interpretation of
Daniel's prayer request (cf. Dan. 9:3). Interpreters' historical and theological biases and
presuppositions drive their understanding of these ambiguous texts!

▣ "there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. . .one week" The seventy units of
seven will be broken into three time periods: one unit of seven sevens (Dan. 9:25); one unit of sixty-two
sevens (9:25); and one unit of one seven (9:27). The crux for commentators has been how these relate to
each other:

- are they sequential

- are there time segments between these three time units

- the text itself does not tell us why these divisions are made

For me this issue is the symbolic nature of the number (i.e., 70) and its previous use in
Dan. 9:2 (the quote from Jeremiah). This number is used of God's sovereign plan for Israel's punishment
(cf. Jer. 25:9-13; 29:10) and restoration (cf. Jer. 30:18-22; 31:38-40). Numerical precision is not
the focus, but divine sovereignty over time, history, and redemption!

For a good, brief discussion of the symbolic use of numbers see

- Encyclopedia Judaica, vol. 12, pp. 1256-1259

- Biblical Numerology, A Basic Study of the Use of Numbers in the Bible, by John J. Davis

- Biblical Hermeneutics, by Milton S. Terry, pp. 380-390

and its temple. To his shock, he learned that there would be subsequent attacks and destructions

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- It is interesting to speculate how many of the earlier writings of the Hebrew prophets Daniel
had read. It seems for sure he had read Ezekiel because he describes YHWH's throne in a similar
way (i.e., "wheels," cf. Ezek. 10:2,6,13 and Dan. 7:9). Many of the words and phrases Daniel uses
are found in Isaiah. In this chapter we are told specifically that Daniel was familiar with the
prophecy of Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 25:9-13; 29:10).

This "seventy years" (Dan. 9:2) can be calculated in different ways.

- from the destruction of the temple (586 B.C.) to the rebuilding of
the temple (516 B.C.)

- from the exile of Jehoiakim (605 B.C., cf. Dan. 1:1) to the decree
of Cyrus for all the exiled peoples to be allowed to return home and rebuild their
national temples (538 B.C., cf. Ezra 1:1-4; Isa. 44:28-45:7).

- The other chapters of Daniel have emphasized the arrogant unbelief of the Gentile rulers of the
Ancient Near East. The Babylonian exile is mentioned in Dan. 1:1-2, but not the reason for it
(e.g., Ezra 5:12). In this chapter Daniel acknowledges his personal sins and the sins of his
people in a fashion reminiscent of the corporate confessions of Moses (cf. Exod. 32:30-32) and
Isaiah (cf. Isa. 6:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

- It is my understanding at this point in my study that Dan. 9:24-27 refers to the Messiah, Jesus
of Nazareth, and that it uses symbolic numbers (7 x 10 sevens) to reveal some future historical,
redemptive events related to the first coming of Christ.

As it is an error in hermeneutical methodology to interpret all of the
details of parables, so too, the details of apocalyptic literature, for they both use
